title: The Trial, the Crucifixion, and the Burial

verses.text: Then the whole council rose and led Jesus away to Pilate.
And they began to accuse Him, saying, "We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King."
So Pilate asked Him, "Are You the King of the Jews?" "You have said so," Jesus replied.
Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, "I find no basis for a charge against this man."
But they kept insisting, "He stirs up the people all over Judea with His teaching. He began in Galilee and has come all the way here."
When Pilate heard this, he asked if the man was a Galilean.
And learning that Jesus was under Herod's jurisdiction, he sent Him to Herod, who himself was in Jerusalem at that time.
When Herod saw Jesus, he was greatly pleased. He had wanted to see Him for a long time, because he had heard about Him and was hoping to see Him perform a miracle.
Herod questioned Jesus at great length, but He gave no answer.
Meanwhile, the chief priests and scribes stood there, vehemently accusing Him.
And even Herod and his soldiers ridiculed and mocked Him. Dressing Him in a fine robe, they sent Him back to Pilate.
That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies.
Then Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,
and said to them, "You brought me this man as one who was inciting the people to rebellion. I have examined Him here in your presence and found Him not guilty of your charges against Him.
Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us. As you can see, He has done nothing deserving of death.
Therefore I will punish Him and release Him."
But they all cried out in unison: "Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!"
(Barabbas had been imprisoned for an insurrection in the city, and for murder.)
Wanting to release Jesus, Pilate addressed them again,
but they kept shouting, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!"
A third time he said to them, "What evil has this man done? I have found in Him no offense worthy of death. So after I punish Him, I will release Him."
But they were insistent, demanding with loud voices for Jesus to be crucified. And their clamor prevailed.
So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met.
As they had requested, he released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and he handed Jesus over to their will.
As the soldiers led Him away, they seized Simon of Cyrene on his way in from the country, and they put the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.
A great number of people followed Him, including women who kept mourning and wailing for Him.
But Jesus turned to them and said, "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
Look, the days are coming when people will say, 'Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!'
At that time 'they will say to the mountains, "Fall on us!" and to the hills, "Cover us!"'
For if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?"
Two others, who were criminals, were also led away to be executed with Jesus.
When they came to the place called The Skull, they crucified Him there, along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left.
Then Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." And they divided up His garments by casting lots.
The people stood watching, and the rulers sneered at Him, saying, "He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One."
The soldiers also mocked Him and came up to offer Him sour wine.
"If You are the King of the Jews," they said, "save Yourself!"
Above Him was posted an inscription: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
One of the criminals who hung there heaped abuse on Him. "Are You not the Christ?" he said. "Save Yourself and us!"
But the other one rebuked him, saying, "Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment?
We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong."
Then he said, "Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!"
And Jesus said to him, "Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise."
It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over all the land until the ninth hour.
The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn down the middle.
Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, "Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit." And when He had said this, He breathed His last.
When the centurion saw what had happened, he gave glory to God, saying, "Surely this was a righteous man."
And when all the people who had gathered for this spectacle saw what had happened, they returned home beating their breasts.
But all those who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed Him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching these things.
Now there was a Council member named Joseph, a good and righteous man,
who had not consented to their decision or action. He was from the Judean town of Arimathea and was waiting for the kingdom of God.
He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.
Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and placed it in a tomb cut into the rock, where no one had yet been laid.
It was Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning.
The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how His body was placed.
Then they returned to prepare spices and perfumes. And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Passion narrative: the trials before Pilate and Herod, the crucifixion, the death of Jesus, and the burial
context.audience: Pilate, Herod, and the crowd in the narrative, and Luke's Gentile readers, who are told repeatedly that Jesus is innocent. The two criminals and the centurion show who responds to Him.
context.setting: The council takes Jesus to Pilate, the Roman governor, who normally lived in Caesarea but came to Jerusalem for Passover to keep order. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, was also in the city for the feast (v.7). The crucifixion took place at "The Skull" (v.33), Golgotha, outside the city walls and near a road, and the tomb was nearby in a garden belonging to Joseph of Arimathea.
context.custom: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, designed to be public and slow. Jews who were hung on a tree were considered cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23), which made the cross an offense to many Jews. Burial before sundown was required by the Law, and with the Sabbath beginning at sunset (v.54), the women had to wait until Sunday to bring spices.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 22 ended with the council's early-morning hearing. Chapter 23 begins with the whole council leading Jesus to Pilate, and ends with the Sabbath beginning and the women resting. Chapter 24 opens on the first day of the week, with the stone rolled away.
context.timelineBible: Psalm 22 stands behind the garments divided by lots (v.34) and the mocking (v.35-37), and Psalm 31:5, the verse Jesus quotes in verse 46, was a Jewish evening prayer. Isaiah 53 shapes the picture of the innocent sufferer numbered with transgressors. The torn veil (v.45) points to the end of the barrier that kept people from the holiest place in the temple.
context.sparkNotes: The council brings Jesus to Pilate with charges of subverting the nation and claiming to be a king, and Pilate finds no basis for them and sends Him to Herod, who mocks Him and sends Him back. Pilate three times declares Him innocent, but the crowd demands Barabbas instead and Jesus is handed over to be crucified. On the way, Simon of Cyrene carries the cross and Jesus warns the women of Jerusalem about the coming judgment. On the cross He prays, "Father, forgive them," promises a repentant criminal Paradise, and dies with the words, "Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit." The centurion calls Him righteous, and Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented, buries Him in a new tomb.

translation.meaning: Luke has Pilate declare Jesus innocent three times (v.4, 14, 22), and Herod does the same (v.15). Luke is showing that Rome found no crime in Him.
To release or let go, the same verb used for forgiving debts. Jesus prays this for the very people who are crucifying Him. Some early manuscripts omit the verse, but the BSB includes it.
A Persian word for an enclosed garden. In Jewish usage it came to mean the place of the blessed. Jesus tells the criminal that he will be with Him "today," without delay.
To entrust something for safekeeping, as when one deposits money with a friend. Jesus quotes Psalm 31:5 and entrusts His spirit to the Father as He dies.

commentary.note: Henry says Herod, who hoped to see a miracle, was "more abusive to Christ than Pilate was," since his greater knowledge made his contempt more deliberate. Of Simon of Cyrene being forced to carry the cross, he writes, "It was pity, but a cruel pity," meant to keep Jesus alive for more suffering. On the women, he says believers should mourn their own sins rather than the death of Christ: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me."

On "Father, forgive them," Henry says the prayer shows that Christ's death was meant to secure forgiveness for sinners, and that their ignorance partly excuses them and makes them objects of prayer. Of the penitent criminal, he says it proves "even great sinners, if they be true penitents" can find mercy. On Joseph of Arimathea, he praises him as one who "had not consented to their counsel and deed," a good man who followed Christ and showed it at the moment it cost him the most.

Gill says Herod and Pilate, who had been at odds (possibly over the Galileans of Luke 13:1), were reconciled by the trial and united against Christ, which he connects with Psalm 2:1. He reads "today you will be with Me in Paradise" as heaven, not an earthly garden, and argues that the word "today" shows Christ's soul went straight to heaven at death. The three hours' darkness was a preternatural eclipse, and the torn veil fulfills Amos 8:9. He takes "spirit" in verse 46 to mean Jesus' human soul and stresses that He gave up His life voluntarily.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 23, but "The Perfect Penitent" in Mere Christianity reflects on why the cross happened. He says the fact that Christ's death put us right with God matters more than any one theory of how it works. His own best attempt is that only a perfectly good person could repent perfectly, so God became man to offer that repentance for us. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: The council brings Jesus to Pilate, who finds Him innocent and sends Him to Herod. The crowd demands Barabbas, and Jesus is crucified between two criminals, praying for forgiveness. He dies, and Joseph of Arimathea lays His body in a new tomb.
overview.settingLine: Pilate's court, Golgotha, and a tomb.

history.t: Pilate governed Judea for about ten years and was known for harshness toward Jews.
Antipas was in Jerusalem for Passover and had long wanted to see Jesus.

customs.t: Rome used it for slaves and rebels, a slow, public death meant to terrify.
Burial had to happen before the Sabbath began, so the women prepared spices later.

archaeology.t: A crucified man's heel bone, with a nail, was found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968.
The church stands over the traditional sites of the cross and the tomb.

overview.discussion: Pilate declared Jesus innocent three times and still gave in. Why do people go along with what they know is wrong?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
overview.author: Luke
overview.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile readership
